reasons: Candidate B is the smaller and simpler version that meets the spec. It sorts once, merges touching intervals with a non-strict comparison, and extends with max, so no special cases are needed. Candidate A uses a strict comparison, which leaves touching intervals unmerged, and assigns end instead of max, which lets a contained interval shrink the result. A also carries extra copying, type annotations and a docstring that asserts quality without evidence. A maintainer can read B and see it is correct; A needs the tests to find its faults.

objections.claim: The strict inequality does not merge touching intervals, so [1, 2] and [2, 3] stay separate, which violates requirement 3. The automated check reports 3 of 5 fail_to_pass tests failing, consistent with this.

This assigns end rather than max(end, current end), so a contained interval such as [2, 3] following [1, 10] shrinks the merged interval to [1, 3]. The fix is a one-word change, but a maintainer would not see the bug by reading the code.

objections.quote: ordered: List[List[int]] = sorted([list(pair) for pair in intervals])
objections.claim: Copying every pair before sorting is an extra allocation and an extra special case. sorted() already returns a new list, and the loop builds fresh [start, end] lists on append, so the copy adds nothing and the input is not modified without it.
The module docstring asserts quality with no supporting evidence, and the code fails the held-back tests. Prose of this kind tells a maintainer nothing that the code does not.

There is no docstring stating that intervals are closed and that touching intervals merge. A maintainer has to infer from the <= comparison that touching merging is deliberate. A one-line docstring would make the requirement explicit without restating the code.

out_of_lane_notes: The automated check reports that Candidate A fails 3 of 5 fail_to_pass tests and 1 of 7 pass_to_pass tests, and that Candidate B has no findings. I did not run the tests myself; I relied on reading the code for the correctness points above, and those points are consistent with the reported failures. The objections I list under correctness are about the code, which is a maintainability concern as well because the bugs are hard to see by reading.
